messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Vuthy was held against his will in a concrete storage room for three weeks, his captors were exclusively men who checked his restraints without warning. The sudden shift in their breathing, the glint of keys, the heavy thud of boots against the wall—all of it imprinted on him. Even now, decades later, the specific geometry of that captivity explains why a single unexpected glance across a worksite can drop his stomach. During the holding, a thick wire had been wound tightly around his neck, leaving a permanent knot of tension that still pulls sharp when his muscles brace. He would come to understand that his body never forgot the weight of that restraint, and the suffocating confinement itself left a lingering queasiness that still rose when he felt trapped in narrow spaces. He had come to believe that the world was filled with men who would decide where he could move. In the months following his release, a simple knock on the door would send a wave of nausea through his stomach, a visceral wave that always preceded a vivid mental reel. Whenever his gut tightened from being alone with men, the captivity memories would flood forward like a film that played over and over. He watched the reel spin, and that relentless visual replay immediately sharpened his guard against the very men whose footsteps first sparked the nausea. The cycle was fast and unyielding: the body’s warning summons the memory, and the memory hardens the warning. The relentless nausea and the tightening cord in his throat forced Vuthy to build a new architecture of avoidance. Every time the fear of male presence spiked, he began planning an escape route before entering a place, mapping his exit doors the moment he walked into a hardware store or a client’s basement. When the memories of the concrete floor started pressing against his ribs, he would deliberately detach himself from the memories, pulling his attention to the drywall in front of him as if it were a screen. He also started avoiding anniversaries, crossing off the calendar with a blunt black marker to keep the timeline unbroken. This careful scaffolding did not quiet the internal alarm. The longer he detached himself from the memories, the more the memories would intrude, leaving him unable to explain clearly to his wife what he had lived through or search for words to describe it. Because he always planned an escape route before entering a place, his nervous system remained locked in readiness, so that sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard. When the film played over and over, it triggered a cascade of physical reactivity that left him perpetually alert at home, proving that the avoidance strategies themselves were only deepening the sense of threat. Now sixty-nine, Vuthy still works as a plumber, crawling through unfinished basements where a fellow tradesman’s approach can instantly trigger a fresh wave of nausea and a familiar ache in his neck. His wife notices how he scans every doorway before sitting at the kitchen table, how the mere sight of a man walking past their house sends him to the window to watch the street. He tries to keep the marriage steady, but the weight of his avoidance has seeped into their quiet dinners, where he will suddenly check the exit sign above their dining room door instead of listening to his wife speak. What finally brought him to my office was the realization that his escape route planning had stopped him from accepting a senior plumbing contract, and he is most afraid that his body will never learn to distinguish a live wire from a long-ago shadow. He hopes, more than anything, to find a way to sit in a room without counting the doors.
